scenes.heading: ER Diagrams
scenes.narration: An entity-relationship diagram is a visual blueprint of your data, showing the things you store and how they connect.

scenes.heading: Core building blocks
bullets: Entities: the objects you track, like Customer or Order.
Attributes: the properties of an entity, such as email or total.
Relationships: how entities link, like a customer placing orders.
Cardinality: whether a link is one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.
scenes.narration: Entities are the real-world things you care about, and each carries attributes that describe it. Relationships wire those entities together, and cardinality tells you how many of one relate to how many of another. Reading these four elements lets anyone understand the shape of a database at a glance.

scenes.heading: From requirements to schema
scenes.narration: You start by capturing what the business needs to record and the rules that govern it. From those rules you tease out the entities and the attributes that identify them. Finally the diagram becomes a physical schema with primary and foreign keys wiring the tables together.

scenes.heading: Conceptual vs physical
scenes.narration: A conceptual ERD stays abstract so business people can validate the meaning without technical noise. The physical model adds data types, keys, and constraints that a database can actually enforce. Moving deliberately from one to the other keeps the design honest before you commit code.

scenes.heading: Turning entities into tables
scenes.narration: Here the one-to-many relationship from the diagram becomes a foreign key. The orders table references customer_id, so every order must belong to a real customer. That single constraint enforces the relationship the diagram promised and prevents orphaned records.

scenes.text: An ER diagram captures entities, attributes, and relationships so the whole team agrees on data structure before a single table is built.
scenes.narration: Getting the ER diagram right early saves painful schema rewrites later, because everyone shares one clear picture of the data.
